en: Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park. At that time, the *Buddhabhāṣita-kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time...
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Bhikṣus, there are two things by which one falls into hell: [the rest of the passage follows]."
First, to claim that things belong to oneself; second, to seek out people with the desire to obtain offerings.
Furthermore, there are two other matters for a bhikṣu:
first, to listen to the heterodox teachings; second, to have great desire and to accumulate robes, saffron garments, and alms bowls.
Furthermore, there are two things concerning bhikṣus:
first, being overly intimate with laypeople; second, seeing a śramaṇa who maintains the precepts well and instead feeling envy toward him.
Furthermore, there are two things that cause bhikṣus to fall into the cauldron of boiling water: [the aforementioned two].
First, constantly dwelling on sensual desires; second, delighting in forming intimate friendships with acquaintances.
Furthermore, there are two other matters for a bhikṣu:
first, having faults oneself yet being unwilling to repent; second, conversely, dwelling on the evils of others.
Furthermore, there are two things by which a bhikṣu shall fall into hell:
first, slandering the Way of the sūtras; second, violating the sūtras and the precepts.
Furthermore, there are two things for a bhikṣu:
First, they have completely violated the precepts; second, they have attained nothing within the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two things for which a bhikṣu should feel regret:
first, wearing the dharma-robes and kaṣāya by force; second, not maintaining the precepts oneself while failing to serve those śramaṇas who do maintain them.
"Furthermore, monks, there are two things that are truly difficult to cure:
first, a mind that is perverse and distracted; second, obstructing others from practicing the path of a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“Why is the word for a śramaṇa written as ‘śramaṇa’?
There are four types who are called śramaṇas:

first, those whose appearance and attire resemble those of a śramaṇa; second, those who outwardly appear to be śramaṇas while inwardly harboring flattery and deceit; third, those who merely seek to acquire service and reputation, being self-important and arrogant; and fourth, those who practice the precepts without transgression—these are true śramaṇas.”
What is meant by one who possesses the outward appearance and attire?

One who has shaved off his beard and hair, dons the Dharma robes, and carries the alms bowl, yet whose mind is not self-governed, who desires only to commit evil and delights in studying heterodox paths—this is what is called a śramaṇa in name and outward appearance only.

As for those who are inwardly sycophantic and deceitful: they walk with slow and deliberate gait, entering and exiting slowly; outwardly their food and clothing are coarse and poor, yet inwardly they desire what is sweet and delicious; outwardly they dwell among the mountains and use grass and saplings for a hut, yet inwardly they lack faith and sincerity; they deceive themselves with self-complacency, yet inwardly they envy the loyal and upright; they solicit wealth and goods from others under various pretexts to establish a reputation for themselves—this is being sycophantic and deceitful while failing to uphold the precepts.

One who does not uphold the precepts merely desires to be praised by others; they act with flattery and sycophancy in private so as to be praised by others, yet they do not reproach themselves or seek liberation. To possess only such an attitude of flattery and sycophancy is what it means to not uphold the precepts.
What constitutes a true śramaṇa?
One who upholds the precepts and practices the Way, who does not begrudge his life or cast off his body, and who seeks neither worldly things nor offerings.

If there is a bhikṣu who practices the contemplation of emptiness, constantly observing that pure dharmas are fundamentally free from defilement, performing wise actions through his own effort rather than deriving them from others, and attaining nirvāṇa within the Buddha-dharma—this one is a true śramaṇa.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“If you wish to seek the Way, you should follow a true śramaṇa; do not emulate those who are śramaṇas in name only, nor those who are śramaṇas through flattery.”
"It is like a poor man who calls himself 'Greatly Wealthy'; he possesses only the name of wealth while having nothing within.
The Buddha asked Kāśyapa, "Should such a person be considered [wealthy]?"
Kāśyapa replied, “It should not.
The Buddha said:
"It is so. Although there are those who bear the name of 'śramaṇa,' they do not practice the dharma of a śramaṇa, like a poor man claiming to be a great wealthy man.
It is as if someone, submerged and drifting in water, were instead parched with thirst and on the verge of death."

Although a śramaṇa may recite many scriptures, possess lofty talent and wisdom, and yet fail to remove his passions and desires, he will die of the parching hunger and thirst of these very passions; because of this, he shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
It is like a skilled physician who, though possessing a full vessel of medicine, cannot cure his own illness;
likewise, one may recite many sutras yet fail to uphold the precepts.
It is like a mani jewel that has fallen into impurity.

Though one may recite many sutras, if one does not uphold the precepts, it is like a dead person wearing gold, silver, and precious jewels; though the body does not uphold the precepts, one wears the *kāṣāya* robe and merely resembles a śramaṇa.
It is like the son of a householder who dresses and adorns himself, wearing fine new clothes that are pure both inside and out;
yet he recites many sutras without observing the precepts—it is just like this.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"There are four types of people who merely resemble those who maintain the precepts.
What are these four?
First, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the precepts he has undertaken, says, "I have not transgressed.
Although he speaks these words, he does so out of attachment, calling himself virtuous.
Second, if there is a bhikṣu who thoroughly understands the profound sūtras and clings to his practice, saying, "This is my own practice.
Third, if a bhikṣu is deeply attached, saying, "This is my own attachment."

"Fourth, one who says of themselves, 'I always practice an impartial mind,' yet remains attached to and fearful of birth and death—this is what is called a śramaṇa praising himself for upholding the precepts.

The Buddha said to Kāśyapa: "The prohibitive precepts (śīla) are formless; they do not cling to the three realms. They are impermanent, without self, without person, without life-force, without mind, without name or title, without transformation, and without an agent who teaches. They come from nowhere and go nowhere; they have no form and no cessation. There is no body to transgress, no speech to transgress, and no mind to transgress. There is no world and no calculation; there is no worldly affair and no place of abiding. There is neither precept nor thought, and there is no destruction. This is what is called the prohibitive precept."
At that time, the Buddha said:
"The prohibitive precepts are without flaw or defilement, nor is there any attachment.
As for the precepts, they are free from all anger; they bring stability and lead toward the path of transcendence—to practice in this way is to uphold the precepts."

To have no attachment to the physical body, no attachment to life, and no delight in the five realms of existence, while fully understanding and entering the path of the Buddha—this is called upholding the precepts.
It is neither in the middle nor at the edge; it is neither attached nor does it revolve. It is like the wind in empty space—this is what constitutes upholding the precepts.
This is called the person of no-seed who possesses a concentrated mind; being without attachment and without self, this is the mark of a celestial being.
One who understands this is said to purely uphold the precepts, not waver from the prohibitions, remain free from self-conceit, and constantly desire to guard the Way and maintain the precepts.
Is there anyone who surpasses such a person?

There is no such person who believes in emptiness who, following the Buddha’s practice, remains unstained; they enter from the darkness of the world into illumination and clarity, abiding nowhere at all, nor remaining within the three realms.
"This is the Dharma of the Precepts.

When the Buddha preached this Dharma of the Precepts, thirty-three thousand devas and humans all attained the stage of Srotāpanna; eight hundred śramaṇas, through these causes and conditions, attained liberation of mind and crossed over to the other shore, practicing wisdom in this manner.
The Sūtra on the Precepts Spoken by the Buddha for Kāśyapa.
